module: Neonatal Cholestasis, Metabolic Liver Disease and Cirrhosis

steps.say: Acute liver failure in children follows its own rulebook, since adult definitions collapse without chronicity or clear encephalopathy. Three pillars hold the diagnosis: sudden liver injury, no known prior liver disease, and clotting that vitamin K cannot fix. Either encephalopathy with moderate clotting failure, or severe clotting failure alone, completes the picture. Memorise these pillars, because every management step hangs on them.
steps.tx: Apply the **PALF Study Group criteria** exactly (the pediatric acute liver failure definition). Pediatric acute liver failure requires biochemical evidence of acute liver injury, no known chronic liver disease, and coagulopathy uncorrected by parenteral vitamin K (PT-INR of 1.5 or above with encephalopathy, or PT-INR of 2.0 or above without encephalopathy). Give vitamin K first and retest, since deficiency alone mimics failure. Meeting criteria triggers intensive care transfer, transplant centre contact and etiology hunting within hours.

nodes.label: Acute liver injury, no chronic disease

steps.say: Do not wait for flapping tremors in a toddler; they never come. Encephalopathy in infants hides behind irritability, broken sleep and inconsolable crying that tired parents normalise. Subtle grade one changes slip past busy casualty reviews daily. So examine behaviour against baseline, question sleep and feeding patterns, and grade low rather than reassuring yourself falsely.
steps.tx: Detect the **encephalopathy challenge in young children** deliberately. Hepatic encephalopathy is subtle and notoriously difficult to detect in infants and non-verbal children, presenting as irritability, disrupted sleep cycles, or inconsolable crying rather than asterixis (the adult flapping tremor). Grade consciousness with age appropriate scales, involve parents as baseline witnesses, and treat any deterioration as raised intracranial pressure until proven otherwise. Early detection decides ventilation timing and transplant urgency.

steps.say: Paracetamol poisoning has a specific antidote, so give it fast and give it fully. The three bag infusion, one fifty over one hour, then fifty over four, then one hundred over sixteen, all weight based, saves lives even when started late. Remarkably, the same infusion also improves survival in non paracetamol failure by calming microcirculatory injury. Never withhold it debating the cause while the liver dies.
steps.tx: Start the **indication for N-acetylcysteine** immediately in suspected paracetamol injury. Intravenous N-acetylcysteine infusion (150 mg/kg loading over 1 hr, then 50 mg/kg over 4 hr, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hr) is life-saving in paracetamol toxicity and improves transplant-free survival in non-paracetamol PALF. Check paracetamol levels against the treatment nomogram on arrival, but begin the infusion on suspicion alone. Continue through the full course unless anaphylactoid flushing forces a rate adjustment under supervision.

steps.say: The brain, not the liver, kills most of these children, so guard intracranial pressure obsessively. Ammonia climbing past one fifty to two hundred warns of swelling ahead, long before pupils change. Hypertonic saline holding sodium at one forty five to one fifty draws water back out of the brain. Nurse the head up at thirty degrees, keep suctioning gentle, and treat fever and seizures as pressure emergencies.
steps.tx: Manage **intracranial hypertension monitoring** as the intensive care priority. Cerebral edema and intracranial hypertension threaten when arterial ammonia exceeds 150-200 mcmol/L, managed with 3% hypertonic saline (target sodium 145-150 mmol/L) and neuroprotective head-up 30 degrees positioning. Avoid invasive bolts where coagulopathy forbids them, using clinical signs, ammonia trends and optic sheath ultrasound instead. Control fever, seizures and agitation aggressively, since each spikes pressure toward herniation.

steps.say: Listing a child for transplant runs on arithmetic, not impressions. The paediatric end stage score blends bilirubin, clotting, albumin, wasted growth and infancy itself into one mortality number. Children under twelve use this score, with extra weight for growth failure below minus two standard deviations and age under one year. Recalculate it as the child changes, because the list order follows the number.
steps.tx: Calculate **PELD and MELD allocation scores** for every listed child. Pediatric End-Stage Liver Disease (PELD) score calculates waiting list mortality risk in children below 12 years using serum bilirubin, INR, albumin, growth failure (below -2 SD of expected weight and height), and age below 1 year. Higher scores mean higher death risk without transplant and earlier organ offers. Update the score with each blood set, since a rising PELD reorders the queue faster than any phone call.

steps.say: One generous adult liver can rescue two lives when split with skill. The left lateral segment, just segments two and three, fits an infant perfectly, while the extended right side serves an adult recipient. This sharing stretches a scarce donor pool without shortchanging either patient. The transplant diagram shows the principle: native organ out, donor graft plumbed in.
steps.tx: Plan **split-liver transplantation** to stretch the donor pool. Split-liver transplantation divides an adult deceased donor liver into a left lateral segment (segments II and III) for an infant and an extended right trisegment for an adult recipient. Infant recipients gain a size matched graft with excellent outcomes, while the adult receives the larger remainder. List suitable infants for split offers actively, because waiting for whole infant donors alone prolongs exposure to death on the list.

steps.say: After the new liver goes in, the immune system must be taught tolerance without being crushed. Tacrolimus leads, aiming higher troughs of eight to twelve early when rejection lurks, then five to eight once scars settle, always paired with mycophenolate and steroids. The rejection pathway diagram shows the cellular and antibody attacks this cocktail suppresses. Monitor kidneys, sugar and tremor, because the drugs tax all three.
steps.tx: Give standard **post-transplant immunosuppression** as triple therapy. Calcineurin inhibitor tacrolimus (target trough 8-12 ng/mL early, 5-8 ng/mL late) combined with mycophenolate mofetil (antiproliferative guardian) and corticosteroids (steroid cover) forms standard post-transplant immunosuppression. Trough monitoring guides every dose change, since low levels invite rejection and high levels poison kidneys. Taper steroids first over months, keeping tacrolimus as the long term backbone with mycophenolate support.

steps.say: Months after a smooth transplant, new lumps in the neck or belly with fever should trigger a different alarm. Epstein-Barr virus driven lymphocyte overgrowth, not rejection, tops the list in immunosuppressed children. The cure runs opposite to rejection: lighten suppression and add rituximab antibody rather than piling on steroids. Check EBV loads routinely, because rising copies warn before lumps appear.
steps.tx: Suspect **post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder** in febrile lumps after transplant. PTLD is a life-threatening complication driven by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV, the glandular fever virus) proliferation in immunosuppressed graft recipients, treated with reduced immunosuppression and rituximab (the anti-CD20 antibody clearing B cells). Monitor EBV viral loads serially in high risk seronegative recipients of seropositive organs. Biopsy suspicious nodes promptly, since early polymorphic disease reverses while late monoclonal disease behaves like lymphoma.
